document.title: Meadows Housekeeping Calendar App — Work Update — July 30, 2026
document.headline: The housekeeping schedule became a responsive calendar application.

workCoverage.coverageDescription: Covers the calendar application's design and construction through July 30, 2026. The document does not state exact session start and end times.

subject.mainFocus: Building a responsive housekeeping calendar from structured employee, location, and assignment data.
subject.description: Detailed build update covering the data model, schedule-resolution architecture, Apps Script services, responsive Day and Month views, cancellation controls, visual redesign, accessibility, cleanup, and the application's functional boundary.

sections.title: 1. Established the data model
sections.contentSummary: We began by separating employee information, locations, and assignments into structured sheets rather than trying to build the calendar directly from an informal roster. Spreadsheet ID: 1It_C3s-4Nwn7bFKt_InO5bblpF3Fo6dJzsF_WwKhnJo Primary sheets: The Employees sheet was designed with fields such as: Employee_ID Display_Name Email Active Assignment_Eligible Role Notification_Enabled Program_Update_Enabled Created_At Updated_At…

sections.title: 2. Defined the regular employee schedule
sections.contentSummary: We identified the active housekeeping employees, their normal locations, and their regular days off. The schedule information included employees such as: Joe — Supervisor Michael — Supervisor Gina — Floater Tanya — Mesquite South Phyllis — Sagebrush Robert Scott — Mesquite North Terry — Juniper South Jamie — Floater Pam — Floater Kevin M — Aspen North Kevin L — Floater Karina — Front Philip — Aspen South Amor — Juniper North…

sections.title: 3. Designed the schedule-resolution architecture
sections.contentSummary: We decided that the app should eventually distinguish between: the normal schedule temporary exceptions the final resolved schedule The planned resolution order is: 1. Read the employee’s regular weekly schedule 2. Read any employee-specific schedule events 3. Apply overrides for the selected date 4. Return the final resolved assignment The main schedule-event types discussed were: TIME_OFF CALL_OFF CANCEL_ASSIGNMENT…

sections.title: 4. Created the Apps Script project structure
sections.contentSummary: We divided the application into separate server-side and client-side files. Config.gs Code.gs DateService.gs ScheduleService.gs SheetService.gs Index.html Styles.html App.html ClientData.html CalendarViews.html DayDetails.html This prevented the entire application from becoming one large HTML file.

sections.title: 5. Centralized configuration
sections.contentSummary: We created a central configuration object containing: const CONFIG = Object.freeze({ APP_NAME: "Meadows Housekeeping Schedule", APP_VERSION: "0.1.0", TIME_ZONE: "America/Denver", EMPLOYEES_SPREADSHEET_ID: "1It_C3s-4Nwn7bFKt_InO5bblpF3Fo6dJzsF_WwKhnJo", LOCATIONS_SPREADSHEET_ID: "16tLQNEfc7OEF6WCX1eYp97_4-gsyB5eUe9s39julHfc", SHEETS: Object.freeze({ EMPLOYEES: "Employees", ASSIGNMENTS: "Assignments", LOCATIONS: "Locations" })…

sections.title: 6. Built the Apps Script web entry point
sections.contentSummary: We created doGet() to serve the application: function doGet() { return HtmlService .createTemplateFromFile("Index") .evaluate() .setTitle(CONFIG.APP_NAME) .addMetaTag( "viewport", "width=device-width, initial-scale=1" ); } We also created an include helper: function include(filename) { return HtmlService .createHtmlOutputFromFile(filename) .getContent(); } The server exposes calendar data through a function such as: function…

sections.title: 7. Built reusable sheet-reading utilities
sections.contentSummary: We created a generic utility for reading a sheet into JavaScript objects. Instead of returning raw arrays such as: [ ["EMP-001", "Joe", true] ] the service converts the rows into objects such as: { employeeId: "EMP-001", displayName: "Joe", active: true } Headers such as: Employee_ID Display_Name Shift_Start are normalized to: employeeId displayName shiftStart This made the rest of the application easier to read and maintain.

sections.title: 8. Added date utilities
sections.contentSummary: We created helpers for: parsing dates formatting date keys formatting time values generating inclusive date ranges The primary calendar date format is: For example: This provides a stable key for grouping assignments by day.

sections.title: 9. Built the schedule service
sections.contentSummary: The schedule service: Reads active employees. Reads enabled locations. Reads assignments within the requested range. Resolves employee IDs to employee names. Resolves location IDs to display names. Groups assignments by work date. Returns a browser-friendly calendar object. A returned assignment contains values such as: { assignmentId: "ASN-...", employeeId: "EMP-014", employeeName: "Amor", locationId: "JUNIPER-N",…

sections.title: 10. Assembled the HTML application
sections.contentSummary: The application shell includes the component files in this order: <!DOCTYPE html> <html> <head> <base target="_top"> <?!= include("Styles"); ?> </head> <body> <?!= include("App"); ?> <?!= include("ClientData"); ?> <?!= include("CalendarViews"); ?> <?!= include("DayDetails"); ?> </body> </html> The include order matters because: App creates the page elements ClientData creates the state and data functions CalendarViews…

sections.title: 11. Built the application shell
sections.contentSummary: We created the permanent interface structure with IDs used by JavaScript: todayButton dayViewButton monthViewButton refreshButton previousButton nextButton periodTitle periodSubtitle calendarContent The app header contains: The period header contains: current month or day title selected-date subtitle previous button next button The main calendar content is rendered dynamically inside:

sections.title: 12. Fixed an initialization failure
sections.contentSummary: At one point the browser reported: Uncaught TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'addEventListener') The cause was that initialize() attempted to attach listeners to elements that were missing or not yet available. We rewrote initialization so it: Finds all required elements. Builds a list of missing elements. Logs a clear error if anything is absent. Stops initialization instead of crashing. Treats optional…

sections.title: 13. Created client-side calendar state
sections.contentSummary: We introduced a central state object for the browser: const CalendarState = { view: "month", visibleDate: new Date(), selectedDate: new Date(), data: null }; The client-data layer handles: loading visible calendar data refreshing calendar data normalizing server responses storing assignments returning assignments for a date The app loads a buffered range rather than only the exact visible day. For month view, it can load…

sections.title: 14. Built Day and Month views
sections.contentSummary: We created a full rendering module: const CalendarViews = (() => { // private state and functions return Object.freeze({ initialize, render, renderLoading, renderError, setView }); })(); This module handles: initialization navigation view switching period titles month-grid rendering day-agenda rendering selected-date behavior loading states error states date formatting time formatting HTML escaping

sections.title: 15. Added calendar navigation
sections.contentSummary: The controls behave differently depending on the active view. Previous and Next move by one month: Previous and Next move by one day: August 1 → August 2 → August 3 The Today button resets: visible date selected date displayed period to the current date.

sections.title: 16. Built the desktop month view
sections.contentSummary: The desktop month view contains two areas: month grid selected-day details panel The layout uses a responsive grid similar to: grid-template-columns: minmax(720px, 1fr) minmax(300px, 360px); The calendar takes most of the available space while the selected-day panel remains wide enough to display assignment details. Each month cell can show: date number number scheduled first employee name remaining assignment count For…

sections.title: 17. Built the mobile month view
sections.contentSummary: The mobile view was designed to resemble the familiar mobile calendar application layout. It includes: fixed top controls Day and Month buttons previous and next controls compact seven-column month grid selected-day agenda below the grid On mobile: assignment summaries are hidden inside month cells date numbers are centered the selected day’s full assignments appear below the month the desktop side panel is removed The…

sections.title: 18. Built the full Day view
sections.contentSummary: The Day view displays one agenda row for every scheduled employee. Each row contains: shift start time calendar label employee name location cancel control For example: 7:00 AM Housekeeping Terry — Juniper South Juniper South Cancel The time column is visually separated from the assignment details. We considered forcing every assignment to fit into one screen by dividing the available height evenly, but decided to postpone…

sections.title: 19. Designed cancellation as an override rather than deletion
sections.contentSummary: We discussed how cancellation should work at the data level. The assignment should not be deleted. Instead, a cancellation should create a schedule event that overrides it. A future event row could resemble: Event_ID Employee_ID Start_Date End_Date Event_Type Reason_Type Assignment_ID Status Notes Example: EVT-001 EMP-011 2026-08-12 2026-08-12 CANCEL_ASSIGNMENT CALL_OFF ASN-... ACTIVE Called off This preserves: the original…

sections.title: 20. Added the cancellation modal
sections.contentSummary: We explicitly avoided browser alerts and browser confirmation boxes. Instead, we created a real modal: The modal was added to App.html with: cancelModal cancelModalTitle cancelModalDescription cancelNoButton cancelYesButton It uses: role="dialog" aria-modal="true" aria-labelledby="cancelModalTitle" The modal supports: opening from a Cancel button closing with No closing by clicking the backdrop closing with Escape confirming…

sections.title: 21. Added cancellation buttons to Day view
sections.contentSummary: Every Day-view assignment received a red Cancel button with assignment metadata: <button class="cancel-event-button" data-assignment-id="..." data-employee-name="..." data-location-name="..." > Cancel </button> The metadata allows the modal to display a specific confirmation such as: Cancel Terry’s assignment at Juniper South?

sections.title: 22. Added cancellation placement to the desktop selected-day panel
sections.contentSummary: You marked the desired button locations with red boxes in the screenshot. We agreed that the right side of each compact assignment row is the correct location. The compact row was redesigned conceptually as: The associated CSS uses: grid-template-columns: minmax(0, 1fr) auto; This keeps the assignment information aligned on the left while placing a compact Cancel button on the right. The listener logic was expanded so the…

sections.title: 23. Created the initial visual design
sections.contentSummary: The first design intentionally resembled a familiar calendar application. It used: light blue header blue active view button blue weekday bar white month cells selected-date highlight right-side details panel mobile calendar-style layout This provided a recognizable starting point before introducing a distinct identity.

sections.title: 24. Reviewed the desktop appearance professionally
sections.contentSummary: We evaluated the desktop screenshot and identified several issues: large unused white area below the calendar calendar width that was too constrained grid lines that were too dark selected-day panel that felt visually attached rather than intentional month cells that were too tall crowded summaries stray horizontal lines inconsistent padding We then refined: page width calendar height panel proportions grid-line weight…

sections.title: 25. Removed the unnecessary fixed desktop height
sections.contentSummary: The earlier design used values such as: min-height: 700px; and: min-height: 620px; These created a large blank white area below the calendar. We changed the relevant containers to: min-height: 0; This allowed the page to end naturally after the content.

sections.title: 26. Widened the desktop app
sections.contentSummary: The desktop application was changed to use approximately: width: min(calc(100% - 48px), 1280px); This gave the calendar more room on large screens while preserving side margins. The month grid and details panel were balanced so neither felt cramped.

sections.title: 27. Softened the month-grid lines
sections.contentSummary: The original cell borders were dark and visually dominant. We replaced individual dark borders with a one-pixel grid-gap method: .month-grid { gap: 1px; padding: 1px; background: var(--border); } .month-day { border: 0; } The neutral background shows through the one-pixel gaps, producing cleaner grid separators.

sections.title: 28. Improved the month cells
sections.contentSummary: Month cells were refined with: shorter height more consistent padding smaller date numbers ellipsis for overflowing text lighter outside-month backgrounds clearer selected-day outline clearer today indicator The final approximate cell height became: min-height: 92px;

sections.title: 29. Improved the selected-day panel
sections.contentSummary: The panel received: its own border rounded corners soft background header background consistent internal padding clean row separators better empty state Assignment details are now presented in a compact hierarchy: employee name location shift time cancel action

sections.title: 30. Harmonized the color system
sections.contentSummary: The earlier interface combined: bright blue terracotta time columns strong red Cancel buttons gray borders The terracotta did not visually belong with the blue interface. We replaced it with a unified blue-and-slate palette. --primary: #315f8f; --primary-dark: #24496f; --primary-soft: #dce8f3; --primary-faint: #edf4fa; --accent: #58758f; --accent-dark: #405b72; --text: #18212b; --muted-text: #667482; --border: #d4dde6;…

sections.title: 31. Restyled the Day-view time column
sections.contentSummary: The earlier time column used terracotta with dark text. It was changed to a muted slate gradient: background: linear-gradient( 135deg, var(--accent), var(--accent-dark) ); color: #ffffff; This ties the time column to the blue header without making every part of the page the same blue.

sections.title: 32. Standardized buttons
sections.contentSummary: The controls now share common rules for: border radius font weight hover behavior pressed behavior focus behavior padding transitions The active Day or Month control uses a primary-blue gradient. Navigation buttons use pale blue-white surfaces. Cancel buttons remain red because they perform a destructive action.

sections.title: 33. Improved accessibility and interaction feedback
sections.contentSummary: The interface includes: modal dialog roles keyboard Escape support focus placement focus-visible outlines hover states active states disabled states aria-busy loading state escaped display text button labels and date labels Dates in the month grid also receive descriptive aria-label values.

sections.title: 34. Escaped rendered data
sections.contentSummary: The calendar uses an escapeHtml_() helper before inserting values such as: employee name location name assignment ID into generated markup. This prevents names or spreadsheet values from accidentally becoming HTML.

sections.title: 35. Reduced stylesheet redundancy
sections.contentSummary: Over several design rounds, Styles.html accumulated: the original styles desktop-refinement overrides polished-desktop overrides day-color overrides additional mobile overrides This caused the file to become difficult to predict because later rules silently overrode earlier ones. The stylesheet reached roughly: The first cleanup attempt still left the original rules plus another theme block appended to the bottom. We…

sections.title: 36. Preserved responsive behavior during the redesign
sections.contentSummary: The desktop overhaul did not discard the mobile design. At widths under approximately: the app changes to: full-width layout no outer desktop margins no desktop card shadow hidden desktop details panel visible mobile month and agenda composition compact cells smaller typography two-column agenda rows At widths under approximately: the time column and typography become narrower and smaller.

sections.title: 37. Final visual result
sections.contentSummary: The finished design now has: a centered desktop application card a cohesive pale-blue header clear Day and Month controls a polished month grid a selected-date outline compact assignment summaries a separate selected-day panel slate time columns red cancellation controls consistent spacing rounded panels subtle shadows responsive mobile behavior The visual progression was essentially: spreadsheet-like schedule → calendar…

sections.title: 38. Current functional boundary
sections.contentSummary: The application currently provides the interface and client-side behavior for cancellation, including the modal and assignment identification. The remaining cancellation step is the server-side write that would: receive the assignment ID create a cancellation event preserve the original assignment refresh the calendar data show the resolved cancellation state We also left several future capabilities intentionally open:…

subject.mainFocus: Stabilizing the inventory application and building reusable product, SDS, processing, and navigation structures.
subject.description: Meadows Housekeeping work update for July 19, 2026: inventory processing, reusable product and SDS views, and stable Apps Script navigation.

sections.title: Overview
sections.contentSummary: Work completed across Milestones 6 and 7 moved the project from a collection of spreadsheet records and experimental pages into a functioning inventory application with validated transactions, permanent event history, live product information, current SDS access, and reusable browser views. Milestone 6 established the processing layer. Accepted inventory requests now update current quantities and create permanent operational events. Invalid requests remain available for diagnosis but cannot change inventory or…

sections.title: Embedded Navigation Problem and Solution
sections.contentSummary: The route map worked, but page-to-page navigation became unstable when Apps Script pages were used inside an embedded environment. Problem Relative links such as ?view=inventory depended on the browser resolving the correct frame and base URL. Links could work when opened directly yet fail, disappear, or replace the wrong frame when embedded. Solution The server now provides one shared appUrl to every template. Navigation links use the complete Apps Script web-app URL and send every request back through doGet(e)…

sections.title: Work Completed
sections.contentSummary: Inventory Processing Implemented Received, Used Up, Removed, Moved, and Count Corrected actions. Verified correct source and destination quantity changes. Created permanent event records for every accepted transaction. Preserved explanatory notes and automatic transaction context. Defensive Validation Rejected unknown source and destination locations. Rejected removals and moves exceeding available inventory. Prevented negative quantities and partial updates. Kept rejected requests out of the accepted Inventory…

sections.title: Verification
sections.contentSummary: Testing covered both successful operating paths and deliberate failure cases. Received inventory increased the correct destination quantity. Used Up and Removed actions reduced the correct source quantity. Moved inventory preserved the total while changing locations. Count Corrected replaced the recorded amount with the verified count. Unknown destinations produced no partial source subtraction. Over-limit removals and moves produced no negative inventory. Rejected requests remained visible for diagnosis but…

sections.title: Current Status and Next Steps
sections.contentSummary: Immediate next work Connect the Product Directory to getProducts() and load active product records from the Products sheet. Link each product card to the reusable Product View with its stable product ID. Add recent inventory events to the Product View. Create the standalone History View with filtering controls. Run a final route, navigation, data, and regression verification pass.

sections.title: Full product pages

Information shown on each page Product image and category Product name and manufacturer Manufacturer product code Container size and inventory unit Inventory product ID SDS revision, source, and verification information Direct SDS and manufacturer-information buttons when available Navigation and presentation The…

sections.title: Inventory browsing and filtering
sections.contentSummary: The product browser was refined so daily use remains focused while products without an opening inventory balance remain accessible when needed. In stock only Made the default product view. Shows products currently present at the selected location. Reduces clutter during routine inventory work. All products Displays the entire active product catalog. Allows products without inventory records to be found. Supports creating a new opening balance. Product filtering continues to respect the selected inventory location,…

Medium clear liner Brand: Highmark Item number: 792083 Size: 33 × 39 inches Capacity: up to 33 gallons Thickness: 0.60 mil Case quantity: 250 liners Packaging: 25 bags per roll, 10 rolls per case Large clear liner Product code: L38582C Size: 38 × 58 inches Capacity: 55–60 gallons Thickness: 2 mil Case quantity: 100 liners Consistent product names and Medium/Large classifications were recommended. These…

sections.title: Apps Script routing failure diagnosed and repaired
sections.contentSummary: Inventory 3.0 could open correctly from Google Sites, but the Open full product page button could then lead to a blank or older-looking page. The failure appeared to be a deployment problem, but the actual cause was inside Scripts.html . Incorrect routing source Inside an Apps Script application, this can resolve to a temporary address containing: Correct routing source The application was already receiving the stable deployment address from Apps Script: The getAppBaseUrl() helper was rewritten to use…

sections.title: Stable deployment workflow established
sections.contentSummary: The difference between an Apps Script deployment and a deployment version was clarified. Existing deployment Edit through Manage deployments . Select New version . Keep the same deployment ID and /exec URL. Preserve bookmarks, Google Sites buttons, and QR codes. New deployment Creates another deployment ID. Produces another /exec URL. Can leave older versions active and accessible. Should not be used for ordinary code updates. Protected navigation rules Do not build internal app links from window.location . Do not…

sections.title: Longer-term application architecture
sections.contentSummary: A central Klinswork URL registry was considered as a way to manage the addresses of Inventory 3.0, Tasker, Email Composer, and the Tool Center. Such a registry may still be useful for internal navigation and future replacement deployments. The more important discovery, however, is that normal code updates should not require any link changes at all. Stable deployment URLs combined with a single canonical internal base URL remove most of the need for manual link maintenance.

sections.title: The larger achievement
sections.contentSummary: Today’s work substantially expanded Inventory 3.0 while also resolving one of the most confusing problems in Apps Script development: apparently changing links that were actually temporary runtime addresses. A complete product-information page system was established. Product filtering became more practical for daily inventory work. SDS access was integrated into product pages. Two trash-liner products were documented for the catalog. The full-page routing failure was traced to its exact function. The entire…

subject.mainFocus: Connecting task templates throughout the Work Queue stack and proving the upgraded workflow through validation, deployment, and realistic desktop and mobile testing.
subject.description: Klinswork Work Queue 2.0 Phase 2 update for July 25, 2026, covering task templates, formal validation, startup-data integration, interface testing, deployment, and mobile verification.

sections.title: Connected Task_Templates to the application
sections.contentSummary: Phase 2 began by turning the populated Task_Templates sheet into a dependable application service. New backend file TemplateService.gs Responsible for retrieving, normalizing, filtering, and sorting template records. Capabilities added Retrieve all active templates Retrieve one template by ID Return distinct categories Normalize active values and priorities Sort by order, category, and name

sections.title: Verified template retrieval before interface work
sections.contentSummary: A compact Code.gs test called TemplateService.gs → getTaskTemplates() and TemplateService.gs → getTaskTemplateCategories() . Verified totals 10 active templates 6 categories Correct IDs and names Correct descriptions and priorities Correct sorting Verified categories Carpet Care Supplies General Cleaning Windows Other General

sections.title: Expanded formal system validation
sections.contentSummary: Validation.gs now treats the template system as a required part of the Work Queue configuration. New validation coverage CONFIG.SHEETS.TASK_TEMPLATES must exist The Task_Templates sheet must exist All seven required headers must be present Complete result The final validation confirmed the configuration object, Work Queue data spreadsheet, all operational tabs, the shared location source, and all 163 active Work Queue locations.

sections.title: Extended browser startup data
sections.contentSummary: WebApp.gs → getAppInitializationData() and WebApp.gs → getStartupData() were updated so the browser receives templates and template categories during initial loading. Application Work Queue 2.0 Units 8 Locations 163 Templates 10 Categories 6 Active tasks at test time 0 Completed tasks at test time 2

sections.title: Rebuilt the New Task form
sections.contentSummary: The former free-text Category field was replaced with a guided, two-step template selection process. Category is now a required dropdown. Task is a new required dropdown. Task remains disabled until a category is selected. Description and Priority receive defaults but remain editable. Assigned To and Initial Note remain available.

sections.title: Added browser-side template behavior
sections.contentSummary: Scripts.html now stores and applies template data throughout the New Task workflow. Browser behavior Populate Category options Filter Task choices by Category Autofill Description Autofill Priority Reset both controls correctly Preserved flexibility Description remains editable Priority remains editable Category is saved with the task Template ID is not stored yet

sections.title: Added a full interface integration test
sections.contentSummary: The rendered application was inspected before deployment to verify the complete template wiring. Checks included Category and Task selects exist Template state is stored Change handlers are connected Templates filter by category Description and Priority autofill Category submits correctly Result

sections.title: Deployed the template-assisted release
sections.contentSummary: After every backend, validation, startup, HTML, and browser integration test passed, a new Apps Script deployment was created and tested directly. Desktop realistic-task test Selected a unit and location. Selected General Cleaning and Vacuum. Used the autofilled description. Edited the description. Changed Priority to Urgent. Added an initial note. Created and opened the saved task.

sections.title: Verified the complete workflow on mobile
sections.contentSummary: The new deployment was tested on a mobile phone using a realistic task workflow. Mobile results Layout displayed correctly Dropdowns were easy to use Category filtered Task correctly Description and Priority autofilled Task creation succeeded Operational impact The task-creation process changed from a long typing exercise into a quick selection-and-review workflow suitable for use while moving through the building.

sections.title: Established a much stronger development workflow
sections.contentSummary: Each layer was proven before the next layer was changed. This reduced uncertainty, made failures easier to isolate, and replaced trial-and-error deployment with controlled system verification.

sections.title: User-experience result
sections.contentSummary: Behind the scenes, Work Queue performs template lookup, filtering, default selection, validation, persistence, activity logging, and interface refresh. The user experiences only a fast, polished workflow.
